div.p: To achieve a timeliness guaranteed computing in real-time embedded systems, an appropriate task model with timing constraints, environment tools such as an schedulability analyzer and a monitoring tool for verification are required as well as a real-time kernel that supports the task model. In this paper, the functions and implementation techniques of the TMO-eCos2.0 kernel and its enhanced schedulability analysis tool those have been developed by the support of Korean army for real-time distributed embedded computing are introduced. The kernel is a modified eCos TM kernel to support the well-known TMO (Timetriggered Message-triggered Object) as its task model. It provides several TMO-oriented real-time scheduling policies and a distributed IPC scheme while its environment supports a task serializer as an off-line scheduling tool for the design of hard real-time systems. TMO-eCos also supports a TMO-oriented deadline-driven power management scheme for energy saving sensor/actuator systems. Other tools for monitoring, verification and high availability are under development. A new project to develop an unmanned helicopter control system based on the TMO-eCos has been launched this year.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time embedded computing has several differences from server-based real-time computing in several points. Since an embedded real-time computing environment usually has a very static task configuration, the execution behavior is highly predictable. This nature enlarges the possibility of hard real-time computing with restricted resources. However, to achieve a timeliness-guaranteed computing, not only a real-time kernel but also an appropriate task model with timing constraints and environment tools such as a schedulability analyzer and a post-monitoring tool are required.

The TMO (Time-triggered Message-triggered Object) model formalized earlier by Kim and Kopetz [1,2] is a well-known real-time object model that can be used for hard real-time systems. With the TMO model, both functional and timing behaviors of system can be explicitly specified and this property leads us to a design of a highly predictable system. To support the unified TMO scheme from design to verification, developments of a TMO-support embedded kernel and its environment have been launched by Korean Army at 2006. Developments of some basic tools and the kernel; named TMO-eCos2.0; based on the TMO-eCos1.0 [4] and eCos2.0 TM have been completed at 2008 and further developments of additional tools to enhance the development environment are in progress now. The rest of this paper is organized as follows.

In section 2, as a related work, the concept of the TMO model is introduced briefly. In section 3, functions and implementation techniques of the TMO-eCos2.0 kernel and the task serializer as an environment tool are presented and in section 4, we will conclude.

div.head: The TMO Model
div.p: The TMO model is a real-time distributed object model for timeliness-guaranteed computing at design time. Figure 1 shows the structure of a TMO instance. A TMO instance consists of three types of object members: an ODS (Object Data Store), time-triggered methods (SpM: Spontaneous Method) and messagetriggered methods (SvM: Service Method). An SpM is actually a member-thread that is activated by a pregiven timing constraint and must finish its periodic executions within the given deadline. An SvM is also a member-thread that is activated by an event-message from a source outside a TMO. Main differences between the TMO model and conventional objects can be summarized as follows.
TMO is a distributed computing component and thus TMOs distributed over multiple nodes may interact via distributed IPC.
The two types of methods are active member threads in the TMO model (SpM's and SvM's).

SvM's cannot disturb the executions of SpM's. This rule is called the BCC (Basic Concurrency Constraint). Basically, activation of an SvM is allowed only when potentially conflicting SpM executions are not in place.

div.head: TMO-eCos Kernel and its Development Environment
Real-time schedulers
div.p: TMO-eCos2.0 now supports multiple real-time scheduling policies. They are the EDF/BCC, LLF/BCC and the non-preemptive FTFS (First Triggered First Scheduled) scheduler. Their usage characteristics are summarized in Table 1.

The non-preemptive FTFS scheduler is used when an off-line scheduling scenario is given by the task serializer that determines the initial offsets of timetriggered tasks so as that all task instances can be executed without overlap and preemption. And in a serialized scenario, executions of message-triggered are allowed only in predetermined intervals. The task serializer will be briefly introduced in section 3.3. On the other hand, the EDF/BCC and the LLF/BCC are normally used when there is no pre-analysis tool or when the task serialization is not possible. This means that the EDF and LLF schedulers are ones for the systems with dynamic execution behaviors.

With these real-time schedulers, two basic types of real-time tasks; time-triggered and message-triggered tasks; are supported by the kernel. SpMs and SvMs of the TMO model are mapped to theses tasks by the TMOSL (TMO Support Library) for TMO programmers.

The timing precision that is used for representing timing constraints such as start/stop time, period and deadline has been enhanced into micro second unit in V2.0 kernel. Although the scheduling is performed every milli-second, the kernel computes current time in micro-second unit by checking and compensating the raw clock ticks from the last clock interrupt.
With these this schedulers, the kernel shows taskswitch overhead of 1.51 micro-sec and scheduling overhead of 2.73 micro-sec in a 206MHz ARM9 processor environment.

div.head: Distributed IPC and message-triggered tasks
div.p: Management of message-triggered tasks is always done in conjunction with the logical multicast distributed IPC of the TMO-eCos. Once a message is arrived via the network transparent IPC at a channel associated with a message-triggered task, the task is activated and scheduled to finish its service within the pre-given deadline. In case that the message includes an ORT(Official Release Time), scheduling of this task is postponed until the time specified by the ORT.

The IPC subsystem consists of two layers. The lower layer is the intra-node channel IPC layer and the upper is the network transparent distributed IPC layer. This layering is for flexible configurations of the TMO-eCos IPC based on multiple protocols.

Besides supporting this basic channel IPC, the TMOSL has been enhanced to support the RMMC (Real-time Multicast Memory replication Channel) that Since the role of an SvM is to handle external asynchronous events, the channel IPC has been extended so that external devices such as an IO devices or a sensor-alarm device can be associated to a channel. In this case, a message-triggered task can be activated when an asynchronous input occurs and is scheduled to be finished within the predefined deadline.

div.head: Task serializer
div.p: Timeliness-guaranteed computing can hardly be accomplished at run time because of the uncertainty caused by resource sharing, asynchronous events and conflicting timing constraints between tasks. An easier way to reach it is to do some off-line analysis from design time with predictable characteristics of tasks such as WCETs and periods.

The task serializer [7] tries to find feasible scheduling scenarios for a node in that each SpM is executed at its exact trigger-time without any delay and preemption based on the given timing constraints. This is done by recasting the initial offsets of all SpMs to avoid overlaps of executions. By considering the slack time of an extracted scenario, possible time-slots for executions of SvMs can be allocated. Once a serialized scheduling scenario is found successfully, the FTFS policy is used.

The task serializer performs serialization under the flowing assumption that the initial offset of each SpM can be adjusted within the time range of [0, p) at design time, where p is the period of the SpM. Triggering times of the subsequent periodic invocations will be fixed by determining the initial offset of an SpM. This serializer has been enhanced from the first version by using a method named task clustering. The key ideas of the serializer are as follows.
For a given set of SpMs, the serializer does the followings.

[Gcd-slot based start-slot allocation] The serializer divides the hyper-period into small uniform slots with length T where T is the gcd of all periods. Since the period of an SpM is an integer multiple of T, the initial offset can be selected from [0,T), [T, 2T),,,,[(k i -1)T, k i T). Of course these slots can be tried in turn, however some heuristics to reduce the candidate slots are used. The selected slot for an SpM in a try is named the start-slot of SpM i and a selected combination of start-slots of all SpMs is called a start-slot combination.

[Well-balanced start-slot combination first] Although in the worst case, whole starting-slot combinations must be tried, however, the number of tries can be reduced significantly by trying well-balanced combinations first. A well-balanced combination is a scenario in that the executions of task instances are well spread into gcd-slots.
[Reduction of start-slot combinations] The number of trial start-slot combinations can be reduced significantly by using the theorem [7] on removal of circularly identical combinations.

Circularly identical combinations are ones such that a combination can be obtained by slot-base rotating of other ones, even though the start slots of SpMs in a combination differ from the start slots on other combinations.

[Eliminating the core co-prime task group] The second type problem reduction is possible by eliminating a task group; named co-prime skeleton [7]; in which the periods of all tasks are coprime with each other and also co-prime with every single task outside the group. All SpMs belongs to the co-prime skeleton can be allocated contiguously from the beginning of the first gcd slot without any influence to the schedulability of other tasks and the tasks outside the group cannot be allocated in the range used by skeleton tasks in all slots as shown in figure 3. Hence the serialization problem shrinks to a problem of serialization of tasks outside the co-prime skeleton group into the remaining range of slots. [Allocating an initial-offset at the earliest possible position in the start-slot] Once a trial start-slot combination has been selected, the exact triggertimes of SpMs must be chosen on their start-slots. Among empty holes in gcd-slots, an initial-offset is determined as the earliest possible position such that all instances can be located at the same position in periodic slots without overlap. It is known that taking the earliest possible position for a task instance is not worse than taking other positions by Schild [5] and Van Hentenrick [6].

[Reduction of task ordering sequences by recursive task clustering] In allocating initial offsets, it's well known that schedulability depends on the order of task allocation. This means that a large number of task ordering sequences may be tried in worst case.

To reduce the number of task ordering sequences, a new recursive task clustering technique has been contrived and deployed in step-wise allocations. A task cluster is a group of tasks such that an allocation of a task affects those of other tasks in the same cluster because they share same slots directly or in a transitive manner as shown in figure 4. That is, clusters are independent of each other in allocating initial-offsets. So before allocating initial-offsets of tasks, tasks are clustered for problem division. In allocation of tasks in a cluster, once the first task has been selected and allocation of the task has been is fixed, it can be removed from the cluster. Therefore, there can be some changes in slot-dependency transitive relations. These means that further recursive clustering is possible at every step of selecting the first task. Since this recursive task clustering is a divide-and-conquer method, the number of task ordering sequences can be reduced significantly. Figure 4 shows this recursive task clustering.

div.head: Deadline driven power management
div.p: The deadline driven power management scheme with the FTFS scheduler has been developed so as to be deployed only to serialized scheduling scenarios obtained by the task serializer because prediction of task scheduling is possible. In a serialized scenario, all executions of SpMs and possible execution slots for SvMs are fixed. Hence slowing down of an execution of a task is possible if there is a slack before activating the next task and a room exists until the finish-deadline arrives. Of course, the scheduler must compensate the kernel time for the loss of clock ticks that has been consumed for changing the CPU speed. Figure 7 shows a scheduling scenario generated by the task serializer and the modified scenario when this power management scheme has been deployed.

div.head: Applications
div.p: To show the stability of the TMO-eCos2.0, an UAV(Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) control system has been developed on a FCC(Flight Control Computer) based on the TMO scheme and has been tested under a HILS(H/W In-the-Loop Simulation) environment. In

div.head: Concluding Remarks
div.p: This paper introduced the upgraded features of the TMO-eCos2.0 and its environment tools. The main features that have been added are supporting of multiple real-time schedulers, timing precision in micro-sec unit and the deadline-driven power management scheme in conjunction with the task serializer for hard real-time computing. The task serializer itself also has been enhanced by using the slot-based recursive task clustering.

Although some more tools such as an interactive monitoring and verification tool are additionally required to complete a TMO-oriented integrated development environment, we believe that our work that covers the range from the design of scheduling scenario to actual computing platform is a step forward to timeliness guaranteed computing.
